 87. We shall now try to trace the history of appointment of the Judges before the independence and liberation of Bangladesh. There is a long evaluation of the method of appointment of Judges to the superior Judiciary under the British rule in India. Process of Indianisation of Judiciary by the persons of Indian origin was initiated and ground norms were laid for appointments in the Government of Indian Act, 1919. Section 101 of the Act conferred the authority to appoint a Judge of a High Court on his Majesty. Sub-section (3) of said section 101 set out the qualifications of a person for being appointed as a Judge of a High Court. Some of the qualifications opened the door of the higher Judiciary for the first time for the people of the Sub- continent with a concept of quota reservation. Under the Government of lndian Act, 1935 sub-section (2) of section 200 provided inter alia, that "every Judge of the Federal Court shall be appointed by his Majesty by warrant under Royal Sign Manual and shall hold office until he attains the age of 65 years". High Court Judges were also appointed in the same manner under sub-section (2) of section 220 of the Act of 1935 but the tenure of office was up to age of 60 years. After independence, on the 26th day of November, 1949 the people of India adopted the Constitution for India that is 'Bharat' a union of States. The Constitution of India was amended more than 100 times but was never suspended or abrogated and thereby maintained its continuity. In 1956, Pakistan for the first time adopted a Constitution, which was soon replaced by the Constitution of 1962 under the patronisation of a General; and by the ones of 1972 and 1973.

At the time the Home Minister was assigned to look after the process of appointment of Judges to the superior Judiciary. Following issuance of said memo the then Chief Justice of Madras, Sir Fredric Gentle resigned from his office and put the memo as one of the reason for his resignation. To consider the memo, a conference of the Chief Justices of the High Courts of India held on 26-3-48, which made several recommendations including that 'every Judge of the High Court should be appointed by the President by a warrant under his hand and seal on the recommendation of the Chief Justice of the High Court Division after consultation with the Governor of the State and with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of India. It may be remembered that at the time no Constitution was yet adopted and appointments of Judges were regulated under the Government of India Act, 1935. The conference of Chief Justices made several recommendations including that one.

According to the Constitution of Pakistan of 1956, 1962, 1972 and 1973 the requirement of consultation with the Chief Justice for appointment of Judges was introduced. 

 102. Justice Amin Ahmed, former Chief Justice of the East Pakistan High Court, has narrated certain incidents about the appointment of Judges. At the time he took pride in keeping the process of selection of Judges as dead secret until it was finally approved by the Central Government. He states, 

 "I must say also, to the credit of the then Government, that not a single nomination of mine was turned down or modified. It should also be stated that so far I remember, no case suffered by default during my time.

An instance is worth mentioning which is to the effect that Justice Syed Mahboob Murshid, the then Chief Justice of East Pakistan High Court, recommended the name of Mr Tayyabuddin Talukder for appointment as the Judge of the High Court and for some reasons that recommendation was not supported by Mr Justice AR Cornelius, the then Chief Justice of Pakistan. The President agreed with the Chief Justice of Pakistan, did not make the appointment and for that reason Justice Mahboob Murshid later resigned. This shows as to how much weight used to be given to the 'consultation' in respect of appointment of Judges, which were being made by the President in the Presidential Form of Government." 

 "Thus within the framework of the law there is room for the development of rules of practice, rules which may be followed as consistently as the rules of law, and which deter- mine the procedure which the men concerned with the Government must follow." 

 "Constitutional convention is broadly defined as rules of political practice which are regarded as binding by those whom they apply but which are not laws as these are not enforced by Courts. It may be an aid to construction but not positive rule of law, breech of which is remediable by the Court action. It must however, be remembered that the conventions grow around and upon the principles of a written Constitution. The conventions generally grow where the powers of the Government are vested in different persons or bodies or where in the words of Sir William Holdsworth, the conventions of the Eighteenth Century Constitution, 17 IOWA Law Review, P-162. there is a mixed Constitution. But conventions do pre- suppose the law and any convention contrary to the written text is of no validity. The conventions are built, in the first instance, on the foundation of law but once these are established they tend to form the basis for the law. It may, however, be noticed that these rules of law which are conventions are mere matter of practice and their effect must change with the changing circumstances of national life ....

 161. Dr Hossain has highlighted the convention over sixty years in the process of appointment of Judges. Dr. Hossain contended, there was no provision in the High Courts Act, 1861 for appointment of Additional Judges of the High Courts with restricted tenure until the Government of India Act 1915 was promulgated. Under the Act of 1915, a. provision was enacted in section 101 (2) for appointment of Additional Judges in any High Courts for a period not exceeding two years. The Government of India Act 1915 was replaced by the Government of India Act 1935. Under this Act of 1935, the appointments of Judges in the High Courts were made at the pleasure of the Crown but the Judges were given security of tenure. It is pointed out that under the Act of 1935 there was no provision for appointment of Additional Judges on the consultation with the Chief Justice of a High Court but, as a matter of convention, the Judges were appointed with prior consultation.

In the Second Judges' case it was observed by Kuldip Singh, J, that prior to coming into force of the Constitution of India the appointments of Federal Court Judges and Judges of the High Courts were made under sections 200 and 220, respectively of the Government of IndiaAct, 1935.  165. In Manabjamins case, Syed Amirul Islam J had extracted the exposition as made in the case of Al-Jahed Trust case while discussing the appointment of the Judges of the superior Courts during pre-partition period. It was observed that under the Government of India Act, 1935, the appointment of Judges of the Superior Courts remained a matter of pleasure of the Crown but the Judges were given security of tenure up to the age of superannuation. The procedure for appointment was that the Governor of a Province used to consult the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned and then used to advise the King through the Secretary of the State of India with the recommendation of the Chief Justice. On the basis of the above advice, the appointments were made by the Crown. This procedure was followed till 4th November, 1947, on which date the then Home Minister attempted to control the Judiciary and issued a memorandum providing the procedure for appointment of High Court Judges. Under this provision, the Chief Minister of a State, acting in consultation with the Home Minister of the State concerned, was to send his recommendations to the Home Minister in the centre. After circulation of the said memorandum there was resistance and consequently Sir Frederick Gentle, Chief Justice of Madras High Court, communicated the Government expressing his desire to resign as a symbol of protest of the said memorandum. Sir Archibala Nye, Governor of Madras also protested the said memorandum. They were of the view that the above procedure would lead to political jobbery and would impair the independence of Judiciary. A conference of the Chief Justices of the High Courts of India was held on 26th March, 1948 to consider the said memorandum in which a number of recommendations were made in the said conference suggesting amongst others, that "every Judge of the High Court should be appointed by the President by a warrant under his hand and seal on the recommendation of the Chief Justice of High Court after consultation with the Governor of the State and with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of India." It has been observed in SP Gupta's case that the system of appointment of Additional Judges was therefore in vogue when the Constituent Assembly met to frame the Constitution. Article 199 of the draft Constitution was almost in the same terms as sub- section (3) of section 222 of the Government of India Act, 1935. 

 "Now we take up the interpretation of the Judiciary-related Articles as mentioned in the Constitution. The first which shall come up for consideration will be the meaning of the word "consultation" which is very pivotal in nature because the whole controversy with regard to the independence of the Judiciary and the appointments of the Judges have close nexus with it or, in other words, deep-rooted in it. In order to find out the true import or meaning of this word "consultation" the whole history of the judicial set-ups in India and Pakistan has been traced going back to the Government of India Act, 1935 and even the period earlier than that as mentioned in the preceding paragraphs of this judgment. It is manifest that in earlier legal instruments before the partition, the word "consultation" is not used because there was no need to mention it as the appointments were directly made by the British Rulers who enjoyed the supreme control and the appointees were at the receiving end. The need was felt to use the word "consultation" in the scheme of appointments in the superior Judiciary in the Constitution when India and Pakistan became independent countries to enjoy the benefit and fruits of democratic rule for which agitation was made by the people who rendered sacrifices of lives and property and millions of them were uprooted and migrated for achievement of freedom. It was made known to the people that they were fighting for freedom and in consequence of freedom what would they gain would be democracy and their own Government and perception of such democracy was Government of the people, for the people and by the people. To set up such democratic Governments, Constitutions were made in India and Pakistan in order to produce system of governance with trichotomy of powers among the three pillars, namely, the Legislature, Executive and Judiciary. The word "consultation" has been used for the first time in the Constitution of India and the Constitution of Pakistan in connection with appointments of Judges in the Superior Judiciary. The history of India and Pakistan, as mentioned in detail in the preceding part of this judgment, very clearly shows that always effort was made to seek that the Judiciary functioned independently and should not be controlled by the Executive. There is no cavil with the proposition that the Legislature has to legislate, the Executive has to execute laws and the Judiciary has to interpret the Constitution and laws. The success of the system of governance can be guaranteed and achieved only when these pillars of the State exercise their powers and authority within their limits without transgressing into the field of the others by acting in the spirit of harmony, cooperation and coordination. Since the proclamation under Article 356(1) was issued by the President on the advice of the cabinet given under Article 74(2) and since sub-clause (2) bars enquiry into the question whether any, and if so, what advice was tendered by the cabinet to the President, judicial review of the reasons which led to the issuance of the proclamation also stands barred. 

 "What is further, although Article 74(2) bars judicial review so far as the advice given by the Ministers is concerned, it does not bar scrutiny of the material on the basis of which the advice is given. The Courts are not interested in either the advice given by the Ministers to the President or the reasons for such advice. The Courts are, however, justified in probing as to whether there was any material on the basis of which the advice was given, and whether it was relevant for such advice and the President could have acted on it. Hence when the Courts undertake an enquiry into the existence of such material, the prohibition contained in Article 74(2) does not negate their right to know about the factual existence of any such material. This is not to say that the union government cannot raise the plea of privilege under section 123 of the Evidence Act. As and when such privilege against disclosure is claimed, the Courts will examine such claim within the parameters of the said section on its merits. In this connection, we may quote Justice Matthew, who in the case of State of UP vs Raj Narain, (1975) 3 SCR 333 at 360: (AIR 1975 SC 865 at p.884) observed as follows: 

 (4) All executive actions of the Government shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the President. 

 320. Under the Parliamentary System of Government, there is no doubt that the decision of the President under Article 95 to appoint a Judge as Judge of the SCB is really a decision of the Prime Minister as per Article 55 of the Constitution and the reasons which have weighed the decision would necessarily be part of the advice tendered by the Prime Minister to the President. In view of the proviso to clause (3) of Article 48, the advice given by the Prime Minister to the President is protected from judicial inquiry but as a convention, the CJB has expressed views regarding the appointment of a person as Judge in consultative form, which formed part of the advice by the Prime Minister. The views expressed by the CJB precede the formation of advice and this advice is protected. It is held in State of Punjab vs Union of India AIR 1977 SC 1361 that the reasons which have weighed with the cabinet in giving the advice would certainly form part of the advice. But the material on which the reasoning of the Prime Minister is based and the advice is given cannot be said to form part of the advice. In this connection, in SP Gupta's case an illustration was given in the following manner. A judgment given by a Court is based upon the evidence led by the parties in the trial Court and in the judgment the evidence are referred and discussed. But the evidence do not form part of the judgment, for the judgment consists of the reasons in support of it and the decision thereon and the evidence on which the reasoning and the decision are based would not be part of the judgment. 

 322.  "Now, if secrecy were to be observed in the functioning of government and the processes of government were to be kept hidden from public scrutiny, it would tend to promote and encourage oppression, corruption and misuse or abuse of authority, for it would all be shrouded in the veil of secrecy without any public, there would be greater exposure of the functioning of government and it would help to assure the people of a better and more efficient administration.  326. The object of granting immunity to documents is to ensure the proper working of the government and not to protect the cabinet or its Minister's or government servant from criticism, however intemperate and unfairly based. If the processes of the government are kept hidden from public scrutiny it would tend to promote corruption and misuse of power, and if there is greater exposure of the functioning of the government it would help to assure the people a better and efficient administration. The reason can have little validity in a democratic society, particularly in the present context of democratic system of government which believes in transparency in every sphere of activities. It is only through exposure of its functioning that a democratic government can hope to win the trust of the people, if full information is made available to the people and every action of the government is bonafide and actuated only by public interest. When ever an objection to the disclosure is raised two questions followed to the determination of the Court namely, whether the document relates to affairs of the State and whether its disclosures would in a particular case before the Court be injurious to the public interest. 

 330.  331. There is no dispute that the correspondences exchanged between the CJB and the Government cannot at all be said to be injurious to public interest. In SP Gupta's case Bhagwati, J observed that the harm that would be caused to the public interest, injustice by non disclosure of the documents would in the circumstances far outweigh the injury which may possibly be caused by their disclosure, because the non-disclosure would almost inevitably result in the dismissal of the writ petitions and consequent denial of justice even though the claim of the writ petitioners may be true and just. It is significant to note that had there been non- disclosure of these documents, a certain doubt or misgiving would have continued to prevail in the mind that the decision of non-appointment of the petitioners as Judges was taken by the Government ignoring the recommendations of the CJB and that this decision was motivated by oblique or irrelevant consideration.

Law requires that even if a document is confidential, it must be produced, notwithstanding its confidentiality, it is necessary for fair disposal of the issues involved in the petitions. 

 333. The government is duty bound to furnish all information to the Court as per Article 112 of the Constitution which provides that all Authorities, Executive and Judicial in the Republic, shall act in aid of the Supreme Court. If the Court desires a document for the, administration of justice the Executive is bound to produce it, except those that fall within the exclusionary rule enacted in the proviso to clause (3) of Article 48. As observed above, State's secret documents and minutes of the proceedings of the cabinet or diplomatic correspondences between the state and another friendly country, national security, public peace, security and good neighbourly, documents relating to commercial activities undertaken by the state in pursuit of public policies of social welfare, etc; the disclosure of which would materially affect the freedom but the documents which the petitioners called for did not fall in any of such category. 

 334. This Court with an anxiety to secure administration of justice required the papers relating to the recommendation or otherwise of the CJB regarding the appointment of the writ petitioners. As per constitutional mandate the Executive is bound to act in the aid of this Court so that the administration of justice is not hampered. According to the views taken above, in the public interest the nondisclosure of the documents would seriously handicap the writ petitioners in showing that there was full and effective consultation with the cm and that the cm recommended for their appointment.  341.  342.  345.  346. The government exceeded all norms in the matter of non-appointment of the petitioners as well as in the matter of new appointments. It is often said that malafide or bad faith vitiates everything and a malafide act is a nullity. A malafide act is by its nature an act without jurisdiction.  358. The judicial redress is available only to a person who has suffered a legal injury by reason of violation of his legal right or legal interest protected by the action of the State or other authority, or who is likely to suffer a legal injury by reason of threatened violation of his fundamental or legal right. This right of judicial redress is personal injury to property, body, a reputation from such violation. A lawyer has a vital interest in the independence of the Judiciary; the profession of a lawyer is an integral part of the judicial system; he being an officer of the Court, sits and practices in Court : he has, therefore, a legitimate interest in preserving the integrity and independence of the judicial system, and if the integrity of Judiciary is threatened by an act of the State he is naturally concerned about it. A public spirited Advocate acting bonafide and not for personal gain or political motivation may file a writ petition challenging an unconstitutional or illegal action of the government prejudicially affecting the administration of justice on behalf of those who are the direct victims of such unconstitutional action. It is, however, to be borne in mind that the persons for whom the relief is sought must be ready to accept it; they must appear and make it known that they are claiming such relief.
